summary: This proposed standard defines a YANG extension for defining metadata annotations in YANG modules. It also specifies XML and JSON encodings for these annotations and the rules for annotating instances of YANG data nodes.

eli5.summary: Metadata is extra notes stuck on a piece of information, like a sticky note saying who edited it. This describes how to define and attach such notes to network configuration data.

questions: how are annotations encoded in json for yang
how do yang annotations work in xml
subtitle: A standard way to define and attach extra notes, such as a last-modified time, to YANG data, in both XML and JSON.

tldr.problem: Network management often needs to attach extra information to individual pieces of YANG-modeled data, but ad hoc annotations risk collisions, poor documentation and broken clients.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7952 defines the md:annotation YANG extension for declaring annotations in a module, and specifies how they are written as XML attributes and as JSON members.
tldr.outcome: Annotations get a module name, a namespace, a declared type and documentation, so clients can discover them and tools can understand them. The RFC updates RFC 6110.

today: RFC 7952 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 6110 to cover the DSDL mapping of annotations.

sections.title: Why YANG Needs Metadata
sections.content:
Some information belongs to one particular instance of a data node rather than to the data model. Typical uses listed by the RFC are instance-specific comments, hints about how a user interface should render data, and deactivating a subtree of a configuration datastore while keeping the data in place. NETCONF's <edit-config> operation already uses annotations, in the form of XML attributes, to say where in a datastore to act and what kind of operation to perform.

Used ad hoc, annotations could cause interoperability problems. The RFC therefore sets four requirements: the set of annotations must be extensible without collisions, their syntax and meaning must be documented, clients of NETCONF or RESTCONF must be able to discover the annotations a server supports, and annotations sent by a server should not break clients that do not support them.
sections.eli5: People want to stick little notes onto pieces of network settings. If everyone invents their own kind of note, nobody can read each other's. This RFC sets the rules for notes.

sections.title: Defining an Annotation
sections.content:
An annotation is declared with the md:annotation extension from the module ietf-yang-metadata. Any module that imports it can declare one or more annotations. Because the annotation lives in a YANG module, it is tied to that module's name and namespace URI, and its meaning is documented by the standard description and reference statements.

The allowed substatements are description, if-feature, reference, status, type and units. The type substatement MUST be present, and the annotation's value MUST match it. An annotation carries a single value, so it is a scalar. Using if-feature makes the annotation conditional on a server feature.

An annotation MUST NOT change the data tree semantics defined by YANG. The RFC's example of something illegal is an annotation that overrides the uniqueness of leaf-list entries.

A module that contains md:annotation statements SHOULD NOT also define data nodes or groupings. Derived types, identities and features SHOULD NOT be defined there unless the annotation definitions use them.
sections.eli5: To make a new kind of sticky note, you write its name, what kind of thing goes on it (a date, a number) and a short explanation. The note can only hold one thing, and it must never change what the page itself means.

sections.title: Using Annotations
sections.content:
A server shows that it supports an annotation by advertising the YANG module that defines it. The annotation can then be attached to an instance of a data node defined in any YANG module the server implements. A client MUST NOT add an annotation the server did not advertise.

Because a client that does not understand an annotation may fail, the RFC says it is generally safe for a server to use annotations in three cases: the annotation is an integral part of a built-in or negotiated protocol capability, it holds auxiliary information that is not critical for protocol operation, or the client explicitly asks for it, for example through a parameter of a request.

The RFC deliberately limits annotations to scalar values, and they can be attached only to individual list or leaf-list entries, not to a whole list or leaf-list. These limits keep the design compatible with XML attributes. A new built-in YANG statement was considered but judged too big a change for YANG 1.1, which was chartered as a maintenance revision.
sections.eli5: A shop only puts a kind of note on things if it has told you about that kind of note. And you should not put a note on something unless the shop says that kind is allowed.

sections.title: XML and JSON Encoding
sections.content:
In XML, an annotation becomes an XML attribute on the data node's element. The attribute's local name is the annotation name, its namespace is the URI from the defining module's namespace statement, and the module's prefix is RECOMMENDED in the qualified name. The value is encoded like a YANG leaf of the same type.

JSON has no established way to carry metadata, so the RFC defines one. All annotations of one node go into a single metadata object. Each annotation is named module-name:annotation-name, and the module name must always be present, unlike for ordinary data nodes. The placement depends on the node:

  • For a container, list entry or anydata node, the metadata object is a new member named "@" inside that object.
  • For a leaf or anyxml, it is a sibling member named "@" followed by the node's name, such as "@foo:flag".
  • For a leaf-list, it is a sibling array named "@" plus the leaf-list name, whose i-th element is the metadata object for the i-th entry, or null if that entry has none. Trailing nulls MAY be omitted.
sections.eli5: In XML, the note is written right on the item like a label. In JSON, the note goes in a special box named with an at-sign, placed next to the thing it describes.

sections.title: Validation with DSDL Schemas
sections.content:
RFC 6110 maps YANG models to Document Schema Definition Languages (DSDL) so that XML content can be validated. This RFC extends that mapping for md:annotation. If the model has at least one annotation, a RELAX NG named pattern MUST be added to the hybrid schema, and the name __yang_metadata__ is RECOMMENDED.

A reference to that pattern MUST be included in every element pattern for an anydata, container, leaf, leaf-list or list node. Each annotation becomes an optional attribute pattern inside the named pattern. Elements for anyxml nodes do not need the reference because they already allow any XML attributes. The second step of the DSDL mapping is unaffected.
sections.eli5: A checker needs to know which notes are allowed on which items. This part tells the checker to treat every note as optional but properly shaped.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The RFC says the mechanism by itself is no security threat, but the security implications of each particular annotation MUST be considered and documented in its definition. An annotation SHOULD be subject to the same or stricter access control than the node it is attached to. Security-sensitive or privacy-sensitive data is RECOMMENDED to be modeled as regular YANG data nodes rather than as annotations.

IANA registered the URI urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-yang-metadata in the IETF XML Registry, and the module ietf-yang-metadata with prefix md in the YANG Module Names registry.
sections.eli5: Sticky notes should be locked up at least as well as the page they are stuck to. Secrets are better written on the page itself than on a note.
